transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Um… I guess I’m here because I’ve been having a harder time keeping my temper at work. I don’t mean to make it sound worse than it is, but I’ve been snapping at people.

There was a safety meeting where I just started yelling before I could really stop myself, and since then some of the younger inspectors seem almost scared to ask me things. I don’t want to be that kind of person, so… I thought maybe I should talk to someone.
When did you first notice yourself having trouble controlling your temper?

I think… it really started after that machinery accident, the one after they changed us to the overnight schedule. I tried to tell myself I was just tired or stressed, you know, not making excuses… but it’s been going on since then. So, about two years and four months now, I guess.
Do you find yourself having repetitive thoughts or urges to do specific rituals?

Um… I don’t think so. Not like rituals, no. I mean, I can get stuck thinking about things sometimes, but I don’t have, like, certain things I have to do over and over to make it feel right, if that’s what you mean. Does that answer it okay?
Do you often find yourself having thoughts that keep repeating in your mind, even when you try to stop thinking about them?

Yeah… I mean, I try not to dwell on it, and I don’t want to make it sound dramatic, but it does come back on me.

Sometimes it’s just a sound, like a cart clanking, or the smell of hot oil, and then I’m right back in that bay. I can see my coworker by the machine like it’s happening right in front of me again. I do try to push it out of my head, but… it doesn’t always listen, I guess. Does that make sense?
Do you find yourself avoiding certain places, people, or activities because they remind you of the machinery accident?

Yeah… I suppose I do, though I try not to make a big thing of it. At work I’ll go out of my way so I don’t have to pass by the inspection bay if I can avoid it. And I don’t really talk about the accident unless I have to.

I used to like going to those industrial-history talks, you know, the ones with old equipment and factory photos, but I stopped. The machinery pictures just… they set me off more than I expected. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Do you often feel like you're on edge or constantly 'on the lookout' for potential dangers?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I try to tell myself I’m being silly, because I’m not actually in danger most of the time.

But even in the break room, I’m kind of watching the doors, listening for any sudden machine noise. And at rehearsal, where I should be relaxed, I still notice who’s moving behind me or where the exits are. It’s like my body doesn’t quite believe I’m safe, even when I know I am.

Is that what you mean by on the lookout?
Do you experience physical symptoms like headaches, tremors, or palpitations when you're reminded of the accident or when you're feeling on edge?

I’m… not really sure. I mean, I’ve noticed I get tense, but I don’t know if I’d call it headaches or palpitations exactly.

Sometimes I’m just sort of aware of my body, if that makes sense, but I haven’t really paid close attention to whether it’s a specific symptom. I don’t want to overstate it. Is that something I should be noticing more?
Has your difficulty controlling your temper or these memories and feelings about the accident affected your relationships with family or friends outside of work?

I wish I could say it hasn’t, but… yes, it has, more than I like admitting.

I’ve missed a lot of shifts, and I know my patience isn’t what it used to be, especially with the younger trainees. I try to be fair with them, I really do, but I’ve snapped or gotten short enough times that they don’t really have me mentor the newer inspectors anymore. That’s… embarrassing to say.

And outside work, I’ve pulled back from community theater. I used to enjoy rehearsals, but lately I can’t count on myself to get through them properly, so I’ve stopped being as involved. I don’t want people thinking I’m unreliable, but I suppose that’s kind of what’s happened.
Are there any everyday activities or situations that you avoid because they remind you of the machinery accident?

Yes… I suppose I do, though I try not to make a big thing of it.

At work I’ll take a longer way around so I don’t have to pass the inspection bay if I can help it. And if someone brings up the accident, I usually change the subject or just say I don’t really want to get into it.

I also stopped going to these industrial-history talks I used to like. That probably sounds a little odd, but when they’d show pictures of the old machinery, it would set me off. So I just… quit going. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Do you ever feel like you're outside of your body watching yourself, or like things aren't real, when you're reminded of the accident or feeling on edge?

I don’t think so… not in that way.

I mean, I can get rattled and sort of not feel fully myself, but I haven’t noticed feeling like I’m watching from outside my body, or like the room isn’t real. At least, I wouldn’t know to call it that. Is that something people usually recognize pretty clearly?
Have you noticed any significant changes in your ability to enjoy activities or spend time with family and friends since the accident?

I’m not sure I’d call it significant… I mean, I don’t want to overstate it.

I suppose I haven’t been as eager to do some things as I used to, and I’m probably less social than before. But I don’t know if that’s the accident exactly, or just me getting tired and not wanting to make a fuss. My family has noticed I’m around less for certain things, I think, but… I still try. I do still care about them. Is that the kind of change you’re asking about?
Do you feel guilty or responsible in any way for the machinery accident that happened?

I… yes, some. I know maybe I shouldn’t, and people tell me it wasn’t my fault, but I keep going back over it.

I keep thinking if I’d pushed harder about the safety checks, or if I’d stopped that run when it didn’t feel right, maybe he wouldn’t have gotten hurt so bad. I don’t know if that’s fair to say, but it’s where my mind goes.
Do you avoid talking or thinking about your feelings related to the accident because it's too upsetting?

I try not to, yes… I mean, I don’t want to make it sound dramatic, but I do avoid it if I can.

I’ll steer away from talking about the accident, especially my feelings about it. And at work, I go out of my way not to pass the inspection bay if there’s another route. I used to go to those industrial-history talks too, which I actually liked, but I stopped because even the old machinery pictures would… set me off, I guess.

Is that what you mean by avoiding?
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

I don’t know that I’ve completely lost interest… I still like things, or I think I do. It’s more that I don’t seem to get myself to do them as much.

Maybe I’m just tired or distracted. I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is. But yes, some things I used to enjoy don’t feel as easy to enjoy lately. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Do you ever feel numb or disconnected from the world around you when reminded of the accident?

Yes… I think so. I don’t know if I’d call it disconnected exactly, but when something reminds me of it, it’s like I’m not fully in the room anymore.

Like a cart clanking, or that hot oil smell… it can put me right back in that bay. I’ll see my coworker by the machine like it’s happening right in front of me again. It passes, but in the moment it feels very real.

I’m sorry, is that what you mean?
Do you try to avoid thinking about the machinery accident?

Yes… I do. I try not to sit with it too much, if that makes sense.

I won’t really talk about the accident unless I have to, and I go out of my way not to walk past the inspection bay if there’s another way around. I even stopped going to those industrial-history talks I used to enjoy, because the pictures of old machinery would set me off.

I know that probably sounds like a lot of avoiding… but yes, I guess I do.
Have you felt like your reactions to the accident have significantly impacted your overall quality of life?

Yes… I suppose it has. I don’t like saying that, because I’ve always tried to be dependable.

But I’ve missed a lot of shifts, more than I should have. And at work, I’ve lost patience with some of the trainees, which isn’t like how I used to be. They don’t really have me mentor the younger inspectors anymore, and I can’t say I blame them, but it stings.

And outside of work… I’ve pulled back from community theater. I used to really enjoy it, but I can’t reliably get through rehearsals anymore, so I felt like I was letting people down.

So yes, it’s affected things. Maybe more than I wanted to admit. Is that what you mean by quality of life?
